sources.entry: Dagu - Powerful Cron alternative with a Web UI. It allows you to define dependencies between commands as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in a declarative YAML format. (Source Code) GPL-3.0 Go/Docker

summary.one_liner: Dagu is a self-hostable workflow engine shipped as a single binary with a built-in Web UI, defining DAG workflows (dependencies, retries, schedules) in declarative YAML as a cron alternative.
summary.what_it_does: Dagu runs workflows defined as directed acyclic graphs in YAML, with steps that can be shell commands, Docker containers, Kubernetes Jobs, SSH remote commands, and many built-in actions (SQL, HTTP, SFTP, S3, email, file operations, and more). It provides cron-style scheduling with timezones, overlap policies and catch-up windows, plus per-step retries, lifecycle handlers, and human approval or input tasks. Each run keeps per-step logs, run history, and artifacts, viewable in a Web UI. It can run as one process (dagu start-all) or scale out with distributed workers that poll a coordinator over gRPC and are routed by labels. The README also describes RBAC/auth modes, Prometheus metrics, an MCP server, and an optional paid Dagu Console monitoring service.
use_cases: schedule and chain interdependent shell scripts
replace cron jobs with retries and run history
run ETL and data pipeline steps
automate remote server tasks over SSH
run Docker containers or Kubernetes Jobs as workflow steps
add approval or input gates to operational runbooks
how_to_run: Open the Web UI on port 8080 and create the admin account
notable: Single binary with built-in Web UI; no external database or message broker required
Declarative YAML DAG definitions with dependencies, parameters, and sub-DAG fan-out
Built-in MCP server for inspecting and controlling workflows and runs
Reusable build workflows that skip steps when inputs are unchanged
Distributed workers that make outbound-only polling connections to a coordinator
caveats: Some features are gated: SSO, RBAC audit logging and Dagu Console monitoring require a self-host license or paid plan; Console monitoring is in beta
Build workflows currently run locally only
Docker socket mounting grants workflows control of the host Docker daemon, so it is a privileged setup
